name: Fireflies
basis: animated light agents revealing the picture (how)

lumenary.blurb: A summer night: the picture sits in near darkness, and each firefly lights up the patch of it beneath, blinking on and off. Keep still and they gather round the cursor.

why: A firefly makes light by chemistry, with almost no heat, and blinks it as a signal. The sky of a summer night, the quiet and a few drifting sparks give a special mood, and a picture seen only by these points of light becomes a place you discover bit by bit. Each one lights the patch beneath it.
how: Give each firefly a position, heading and its own rhythm, and let the heading drift smoothly: its rate of change is 5 × (n − ½) where n is slow noise.
Move it at the speed set by the slider with a slight upward float, and let it re-enter at the opposite edge.
When the pointer is in the picture, pull fireflies in: within half the picture’s width the pull is 55 px per second at the pointer, falling off linearly.
Blink each on its own period of 1.4 to 3.8 seconds and its own phase, with brightness b = lerp(1, w^2.2, blink).
Darken the picture by the night value and add a soft glow from each firefly, revealing the picture beneath.
history: Fireflies produce light with luciferin and the enzyme luciferase in a reaction that gives off very little heat. In Japan, hotaru-gari, going to watch fireflies, has been a summer pastime for centuries. Some species in Southeast Asia and in the Great Smoky Mountains blink together, a synchrony that biologists and mathematicians such as Steven Strogatz have studied as an example of coupled oscillators.
uses: Atmospheric scenes in film, games and websites
terms: Light produced by a living thing through chemistry.
The enzyme that makes fireflies glow.
Rhythms that influence each other and can fall into step.
paragraphs: On a summer night the picture sits in near darkness, and each firefly lights the patch of it beneath. Every firefly has a position, a heading and its own rhythm. The heading drifts smoothly: its rate of change is 5 × (n − ½) where n is slow noise, so the flight curves lazily, and the speed is set by the slider with a slight upward float. Fireflies leave one edge and re-enter at the opposite one. When the pointer is inside the picture it draws them in: within half the picture’s width the pull is 55 px per second at the pointer and falls off linearly with distance. Each blinks on its own period of 1.4 to 3.8 seconds and its own phase, with a brightness b = lerp(1, w^2.2, blink), where w = ½ + ½ sin(2πt/T + φ); the power makes each flash short and the dark between them long.

The lighting is built in layers. First a near-black field with the picture at a fraction 1 − night of its brightness. Then a mask is painted: each firefly stamps a soft radial sprite (radius 30 to 125 px times 0.6 to 1.1, according to its brightness) at an opacity equal to b, and stamps combine as 1 − Π(1 − bᵢ gᵢ), so overlapping lights add up without ever exceeding 1. The sharp picture seen through this mask is added to the dark base with additive blending. Last, each firefly draws a small halo in its colour (green-gold, amber, cool white or pink) and a bright white core, also additively.

equations.note: A firefly’s heading a and velocity: n is slow noise, s the firefly’s own offset and κ its personal speed factor (0.6 to 1.4).
The blinking: β is the blinking slider, T the firefly’s period and φ its phase.
The light mask m, and the final colour: g and h are the radial profiles of the mask and halo sprites, c the firefly colour.

presets.text: A few amber fireflies on a very dark night feel like embers.
A big swarm with strong blinking gives a festival.
Pink and wide glow looks like a fairytale.
